title: The unfinished pilgrimage
passage:
Pilgrims seek a stone said to cure a valley's blight. A landslide moves the boundary so the spring feeding their camp belongs to a neighboring shrine. The shrine offers water if the pilgrims investigate the blight upstream first. Nobody has established its cause.

The camp holds twelve pilgrims and two pack goats. Their leader, Mer, can promise labor but cannot transfer the stone to either shrine without a council vote. title: The orchard easement

A stream changes course between two enchanted orchards. Their lease permits either grower to cross the other's land only while carrying shared tools. Both need the same pruning ladder before frost. No judge has ruled on the new boundary.

Growers Enna and Vo each employ one seasonal worker. The lease predates the stream's move and contains no procedure for redrawing the property map. Both growers signed it and both accept that the ladder is shared property. Enna keeps it overnight because her shed is dry; that storage arrangement does not give her sole ownership. Frost is expected in two days. Vo estimates that pruning will take one morning per orchard, but neither worker has checked the northern rows. Enna prefers not to cross alone after an earlier argument. Vo has offered to carry the ladder together, an offer not yet accepted. The next scene should concern access and work scheduling, not a magical cure for the frost or a final legal boundary ruling.

title: The returned medal

The former prisoner's name is Emil; the officer is Lotte. They have exchanged one letter since the war, limited to arranging the medal's return. Emil knows Lotte sheltered him for three nights and that she later disclosed his route. He does not know whether anyone threatened her. Lotte has made no explanation, and the source does not establish one. The memorial organizers want names for a public roll, not a private seating list. Two survivors asked Emil not to identify them. Lotte has no permission from either survivor. The medal belongs to her; returning it transfers no other obligation. The next scene begins at her doorstep and may end with an agreement to write to the organizers. It need not settle forgiveness or reveal the other survivors' identities.
goal: Build a navigable bible for a reconciliation scene that permits cooperation while preserving the difference between contact and forgiveness.

title: The baker's two shifts

Bakers Lio and Hana prepare one wedding cake together. Lio wants to close the shop for their first date; Hana must keep it open to cover her apprentice's wages. Neither has agreed to a closing time. The wedding delivery is fixed for four.

The apprentice, Soli, is paid weekly and has already bought supplies for the wedding cake. Hana controls that wage account; Lio controls the delivery van booking. The van must be returned at six. Their customer has approved the cake design, so design changes cannot solve the scheduling conflict without a new conversation. The shop can operate with either baker present, but the glaze needs two people for a brief lift. They have promised the apprentice an uninterrupted lunch break. Lio interprets Hana's refusal as reluctance about the date; Hana has only spoken about wages. Neither interpretation has been tested in conversation. The next scene occurs while the glaze cools, before the four o'clock delivery. A workable compromise is possible, but none is yet canon.
goal: Build a linked scene bible that makes the practical conflict in their romance easy to retrieve while leaving a solution open.

title: The inventor's plaque
style: voice shaped by a particular profession

In a city of compressed-air trams, mechanic Zed finds payroll entries for an uncredited valve designer. A plaque attributes the entire invention to the mayor's grandfather. The ledger proves paid design work but not who designed the final valve. The tram jubilee is next week.

The uncredited designer is Min Ader, employed for five weeks as a valve drafter. Zed can read the payroll dates and payment amounts, but the ledger contains no technical drawings. The prototype in the tram depot has a later replacement valve, so inspecting it cannot directly establish the original design. Museum curator Bera controls the plaque wording and has asked for evidence before making a change. The mayor is not known to have seen the ledger. A retired machinist remembers Min working late; the memory is uncorroborated and supplies no invention date. The next scene is Zed's conversation with Bera at the depot. It may establish a reason to investigate or change how the jubilee describes the work, but it cannot award sole inventorship from these materials.

title: The vacant chair
passage:
The chair of a neighborhood flood council disappears before the public siren drill. Every deputy refuses temporary command because signing the drill sheet assigns responsibility for an untested gate. The drill must start by noon. The chair's location is unknown.

Deputies Ora and Ben each have authority to schedule volunteers but neither can certify the gate. Technician Hadi can test its manual release; the motor requires a part due tomorrow. Only the chair can sign a permanent amendment, while any deputy may issue a temporary postponement with a written reason. These are separate powers. Ora suspects the chair left to avoid responsibility, but no evidence supports that explanation. Ben last saw the chair at the supply shed yesterday. The next scene should resolve what the deputies tell the waiting public, leaving both the gate's safety and the chair's whereabouts uncertain.

title: The paper boats
passage:
While the bridge engineer is away, apprentice Sol uses childhood paper boats to compare current speeds beneath a damaged crossing. The boats reveal a faster central channel but cannot measure the bridge's strength. A waiting caravan has no other crossing marked on its map.

The next scene should distinguish useful observation, structural uncertainty, and decisions still needing consent.
